author: EmuCore - Hub
title: mGBA’s ARM debugger now exposes processor mode and SPSR state
summary: The command-line debugger already printed packed ARM program-status bits, but users still had to decode the privileged mode and inspect banked state indirectly. mGBA now labels the PSR mode and includes the saved PSR register in its register listing.
heroAlt: Close-up photograph of the Game Boy Advance processor.

blocks.text: Status bits describe more than condition flags

The ARM program status register contains condition flags such as N, Z, C, and V, along with interrupt masks, execution state, and a processor-mode field. A hexadecimal dump preserves every bit but makes the active privilege mode difficult to recognize during a debugging session, especially when investigating exception entry or a mode switch.
Print a readable name for each defined mode

The merged mGBA change adds a helper that maps the PSR privilege field to short labels: user, FIQ, IRQ, supervisor, abort, undefined, and system. The existing flag display remains, with the mode name appended to the same status-register line; encodings that do not match a defined mode are shown as invalid instead of being misnamed.

Some ARM modes maintain an SPSR that records status when an exception is taken. The CLI register listing now prints SPSR alongside the current PSR, exposing banked exception state that matters when stepping through handler entry and return. It gives a debugger user a direct value to inspect rather than requiring an indirect inference from the current flags.
A debugger view improves diagnosis, not execution

This is a visibility improvement in the command-line debugger; it does not change CPU execution or the register values stored by the emulator. A focused check should enter representative modes, compare labels against the packed mode bits, inspect SPSR around an exception, and confirm that the new output remains readable in the debugger’s existing register listing.
